scenes.tts: Chapter one ended on a clue: add protein and see whether a spot grows bigger or brighter. Now meet the bodies and chromatin a real nucleus holds. Which have been tested as liquids, and what did those tests show?
scenes.narration: Chapter one ended on a clue: add protein and see whether a spot grows bigger or brighter. Now meet the bodies and chromatin a real nucleus holds. Which have been tested as liquids, and what did those tests show?
scenes.caption: Chapter one ended on a clue: add protein and see whether a spot grows bigger or brighter. Now meet the bodies and chromatin a real nucleus holds. Which have been tested as liquids, and what did those tests show?
scenes.visual: THE WORLD, carried from chapter 1 (16:9) but now ONE large cutaway nucleus, a soft GREY-outlined circle about 80% of frame height, centred. Carry chapter 1's COLOUR MAP and add GREEN = RNA: BLUE = protein molecules; TEAL = droplets, the dense phase; ORANGE = binding sites; YELLOW = the saturation concentration; PURPLE = DNA and chromatin; GREEN = RNA; GREY = outlines and leader lines; white = words. Small corner label 'schematic'. Opening frame: chapter 1's two nuclei, shrunk, side by side, with their labels 'bigger, not brighter' (TEAL) and 'brighter, not bigger' (ORANGE) and the dial between them. On 'Now meet', the two small nuclei slide together and merge into the one large nucleus; the dial shrinks to a small GREY icon in the top-left corner. Inside the large nucleus about 40 BLUE dots drift (as in chapter 1) and five soft white-blue glows of different sizes fade in at scattered places (the microscope view). On 'tested as liquids', a small white '?' hovers over each glow in turn. On 'what did those tests show?', all the '?' marks pulse once together.
Title 'Real Bodies, Real Tests' fades in across the top for 2 s; blue dots keep drifting and the glows pulse gently. The '?' marks fade out.

scenes.tts: Some order needs no spot at all. After a cell divides, each chromosome partly unpacks but keeps a region of its own: a chromosome territory. Picture balls of yarn in a box, with loose loops poking across where two meet.
scenes.narration: Some order needs no spot at all. After a cell divides, each chromosome partly unpacks but keeps a region of its own: a chromosome territory. Picture balls of yarn in a box, with loose loops poking across where two meet.
scenes.caption: Some order needs no spot at all. After a cell divides, each chromosome partly unpacks but keeps a region of its own: a chromosome territory. Picture balls of yarn in a box, with loose loops poking across where two meet.
scenes.visual: The glows dim to 30%. Show, then name: behind them, three large soft PURPLE regions in three tints (light, mid, deep) grow out from three points until together they fill most of the nucleus, each region a loosely coiled thread. On 'chromosome territory', the label 'chromosome territory' appears with a leader line to the mid-tint region. On 'balls of yarn', each region briefly gains a faint yarn-ball texture. On 'loose loops', zoom slightly into the border between two regions: a few loops of the light PURPLE thread poke into the deep PURPLE region and wave slowly; label 'loops poke across'. Zoom back out as the scene ends.

scenes.tts: A sequencing method called high C maps which stretches of chromatin touch. Its maps reveal two broad compartments. A is open and mostly active. B is closed and mostly quiet, often against a mesh under the nuclear envelope. Standard maps average over millions of cells, not one nucleus.
scenes.narration: A sequencing method called Hi-C maps which stretches of chromatin touch. Its maps reveal two broad compartments. A is open and mostly active. B is closed and mostly quiet, often against a mesh under the nuclear envelope. Standard maps average over millions of cells, not one nucleus.
scenes.caption: A sequencing method called Hi-C maps which stretches of chromatin touch. Its maps reveal two broad compartments. A is open and mostly active. B is closed and mostly quiet, often against a mesh under the nuclear envelope. Standard maps average over millions of cells, not one nucleus.
scenes.visual: The territories stay. Along each PURPLE thread, short segments light up in two shades: open, loosely looped segments turn BRIGHT PURPLE with label 'A: open, mostly active'; tightly packed segments turn DARK PURPLE with label 'B: closed, mostly quiet'. Pairs of segments that lie close in space are joined briefly by thin white arcs that blink on and off (each arc = 'these two touched'); small label 'Hi-C: which parts touch'. On 'a mesh', a thin GREY lattice band draws itself just inside the nuclear outline, labelled 'lamina'; several DARK PURPLE B segments drift outward and settle against it. Labels at most 5 words each. On 'millions of cells', the nucleus is briefly copied into a fanned stack of about twenty faint ghost nuclei receding behind it, each with its white arcs in slightly different places; the arcs from all of them pool into one blurred average pattern drawn over the front nucleus (schematic). On 'one nucleus', the ghosts fold back into the single nucleus and its arcs fade. At the end of the scene the PURPLE territories dim to 40% and the five glows brighten back to full.

scenes.tts: Now the bodies. The nucleolus forms around repeated genes for ribosomal RNA. Mammalian nucleoli have three parts along an inside-out assembly line. Fibrillar centres hold the genes and copying machinery. New RNA emerges at their borders, where processing begins. The outer granular component assembles ribosomal subunits.
scenes.narration: Now the bodies. The nucleolus forms around repeated genes for ribosomal RNA. Mammalian nucleoli have three parts along an inside-out assembly line. Fibrillar centres hold the genes and copying machinery. New RNA emerges at their borders, where processing begins. The outer granular component assembles ribosomal subunits.
scenes.caption: Now the bodies. The nucleolus forms around repeated genes for ribosomal RNA. Mammalian nucleoli have three parts along an inside-out assembly line. Fibrillar centres hold the genes and copying machinery. New RNA emerges at their borders, where processing begins. The outer granular component assembles ribosomal subunits.
scenes.visual: The largest glow, low in the nucleus, grows to about a third of the frame height. It sharpens into one broad GREY granular component containing several small fibrillar centres, each wrapped by dense fibrillar component (still grey: their material nature is not yet claimed). On 'repeated genes', short PURPLE strands with repeated blocks enter the fibrillar centres. On 'inside-out', a white arrow sweeps from one fibrillar centre, across its dense fibrillar component, into the granular component; label 'assembly line'. Then label the parts as the narrator reaches them: 'fibrillar centre: genes, machinery'; 'dense fibrillar component: processing'; 'granular component: assembly'. GREEN RNA threads begin at the borders of the fibrillar centres, pass through the dense fibrillar component, and are processed before small grey ribosomal-subunit particles assemble in the granular component and drift toward the nuclear edge.

scenes.tts: Smaller bodies sit around it, each known by what it holds. Speckles hold splicing factors; Cajal bodies, the marker protein coilin; PML bodies, the PML protein. Paraspeckles are built on a long RNA called neat one.
scenes.narration: Smaller bodies sit around it, each known by what it holds. Speckles hold splicing factors; Cajal bodies, the marker protein coilin; PML bodies, the PML protein. Paraspeckles are built on a long RNA called NEAT1.
scenes.caption: Smaller bodies sit around it, each known by what it holds. Speckles hold splicing factors; Cajal bodies, the marker protein coilin; PML bodies, the PML protein. Paraspeckles are built on a long RNA called NEAT1.
scenes.visual: The nucleolus shrinks back a little; its three detailed labels fade into one label, 'nucleolus'. The four other glows sharpen one by one as each is named, each gaining a white label and a small icon of its contents: 'speckles: splicing factors' (several irregular BLUE blobs); 'Cajal body: coilin' (one round BLUE body); 'PML body: PML protein' (a BLUE ring-shaped body with dots on its rim); 'paraspeckle: NEAT1 RNA' (an elongated body with a thin GREEN RNA thread running along its length). No molecular structures: labelled cartoons only. At most 5 labels remain on screen.

scenes.tts: These bodies are real. They exchange molecules with the nucleoplasm, and several help with a job. But how does each one form? Only a few have had their material properties tested closely.
scenes.narration: These bodies are real. They exchange molecules with the nucleoplasm, and several help with a job. But how does each one form? Only a few have had their material properties tested closely.
scenes.caption: These bodies are real. They exchange molecules with the nucleoplasm, and several help with a job. But how does each one form? Only a few have had their material properties tested closely.
scenes.visual: BLUE dots stream in and out of every body at a steady trickle (exchange). On 'help with a job', small white tick marks appear beside the nucleolus and the speckles. On 'how does each one form?', a white '?' appears over every body. On 'tested closely', the chapter-one dial dims. White outlines pick out the nucleolus and one deep PURPLE heterochromatin patch; the other bodies dim and keep their '?'.

scenes.tts: The strongest liquid-phase evidence here comes from the nucleolus in the egg-forming cells of a frog. Its dense fibrillar and granular components behave like two liquids that coexist without mixing. What should purified nucleolar proteins do when mixed with RNA in a tube?
scenes.narration: The strongest liquid-phase evidence here comes from the nucleolus in the egg-forming cells of a frog. Its dense fibrillar and granular components behave like two liquids that coexist without mixing. What should purified nucleolar proteins do when mixed with RNA in a tube?
scenes.caption: The strongest liquid-phase evidence here comes from the nucleolus in the egg-forming cells of a frog. Its dense fibrillar and granular components behave like two liquids that coexist without mixing. What should purified nucleolar proteins do when mixed with RNA in a tube?
scenes.visual: Zoom into the nucleolus until it fills about 70% of the frame; a small white tag 'frog oocyte nucleolus' sits above it. The dense fibrillar regions and surrounding granular component shift from GREY to two TEAL tints (pale TEAL inside, deep TEAL outside). They wobble gently like liquids and their shared edges ripple, but the two tints never blend. On 'without mixing', label 'two liquids, unmixed'. On 'mixed with RNA', a GREY test tube slides in at the right holding a clear fluid with a mixed cloud of pale and deep TEAL dots and a few thin GREEN RNA threads, labelled 'purified proteins + RNA'. A question card appears top centre: 'What forms in the tube?'
Predict pause, 4.5 s. The question card 'What forms in the tube?' stays on screen. Near-stillness by design: the dots in the test tube drift slowly, the nucleolus layers shimmer, nothing new appears.

scenes.tts: They reproduce the layering: drops with one phase inside the other. This is strong evidence that the frog nucleolus contains coexisting liquid phases.
scenes.narration: They reproduce the layering: drops with one phase inside the other. This is strong evidence that the frog nucleolus contains coexisting liquid phases.
scenes.caption: They reproduce the layering: drops with one phase inside the other. This is strong evidence that the frog nucleolus contains coexisting liquid phases.
scenes.visual: The question card fades. In the test tube, the dots gather into a few small drops, each a pale TEAL core wrapped in a deep TEAL shell, matching the nucleolus regions beside it (schematic). A white '=' sign appears between tube and nucleolus. On 'strong evidence', a white tag 'strong liquid evidence' appears over the frog nucleolus; the tube slides away.

scenes.tts: Heterochromatin, densely packed and mostly silent chromatin, adds a third mechanism. A protein can bridge distant stretches until the fibre collapses into a compact ball. Physicists count that as a phase transition of the chromatin. But it makes a ball of chromatin, not a liquid drop of protein.

Physicists count that as a phase transition of the chromatin. But it makes a ball of chromatin, not a liquid drop of protein.

scenes.visual: Zoom back out to the whole nucleus, then into the deep PURPLE patch outlined in the previous scene: one long loose PURPLE fibre. Next to the TEAL droplet and ORANGE sites icons (small, upper left, from chapter 1), a third icon appears labelled 'bridging'. On 'bridge distant stretches', simple BLUE bridge markers each connect two distant points of the fibre with thin lines; label the markers 'schematic', not molecular structures. Each connection pulls the points together, and over the scene the fibre folds into a compact PURPLE ball with blue markers at its crossings. On 'phase transition', small label 'chromatin collapse'. On 'not a liquid drop', a small TEAL droplet appears beside the ball for contrast, with labels 'ball of chromatin' (PURPLE) and 'drop of protein' (TEAL); the droplet then fades.

scenes.tts: The verdict splits by system. In early fruit fly embryos, foci of HP1a looked liquid-like. In mouse fibroblasts, half-body FRAP found no preferential mixing inside heterochromatin clusters, favouring collapsed chromatin.
scenes.narration: The verdict splits by system. In early fruit fly embryos, foci of HP1a looked liquid-like. In mouse fibroblasts, half-body FRAP found no preferential mixing inside heterochromatin clusters, favouring collapsed chromatin.
scenes.caption: The verdict splits by system. In early fruit fly embryos, foci of HP1a looked liquid-like. In mouse fibroblasts, half-body FRAP found no preferential mixing inside heterochromatin clusters, favouring collapsed chromatin.
scenes.visual: The frame splits into two panels, divider down the middle. LEFT panel, tag 'fly embryo': a round BLUE-filled focus with a soft TEAL rim that wobbles and shimmers; label 'liquid-like'. RIGHT panel, tag 'mouse fibroblast': the compact PURPLE ball from the last scene. On 'half-body FRAP', a white flash darkens the left half of the PURPLE ball. During recovery, BLUE protein dots enter the bleached half from the surrounding nucleoplasm while the unbleached half stays bright: no preferential flow from one half to the other. Labels read 'no internal mixing' and then 'favours collapsed chromatin'. Mark the recovery 'schematic'; claim no recovery rate. At the end of the scene both panels shrink to sit side by side under the white words 'one system each'.

scenes.tts: Neither study speaks for all heterochromatin. Whether phase separation builds a given body in a given living cell is still contested. The text below shows where the test itself grows weaker.
scenes.narration: Neither study speaks for all heterochromatin. Whether phase separation builds a given body in a given living cell is still contested. The text below shows where the test itself grows weaker.
scenes.caption: Neither study speaks for all heterochromatin. Whether phase separation builds a given body in a given living cell is still contested. The text below shows where the test itself grows weaker.
scenes.visual: The two panels sit briefly, then become the whole nucleus again: territories in PURPLE tints, the three-part nucleolus, the four smaller bodies with their one-word labels, BLUE dots trickling in and out. On 'Neither study', the two panels fold back. On 'still contested', a small white '?' returns over every body except the frog-nucleolus tag, which keeps 'strong liquid evidence'. On 'The text below', the labels dim and drift toward the bottom edge.

End card, 4.5 s. The world dims behind. Centred, large, in white: 'Nuclear bodies are real; how each forms is tested body by body.' with 'body by body' emphasised. The territories and bodies keep shimmering faintly behind.
